A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work despite the changed title and framing. Their shared method, experiments, and results establish continuity. Main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, generalization tests, intermediate-decoding results, reward-sampling ablations, training curves, and generated examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds a pretrained process-reward-model comparison, component ablations, runtime measurements, failure analyses, and qualitative examples.

M1.justification: SAPO is reframed as denoising process rewards, but the implemented procedure remains the same: compare intermediate-completion accuracy with reused initial rollouts, add the process reward when the original advantage is positive, and append 64 masks for intermediate completions. v2's full-reward formalization and ablation variants do not establish a change to the default algorithm.

E1.justification: GSM8K, MATH, COUNTDOWN, SUDOKU, and the SVAMP/ARC generalization evaluations remain. Removing the s1K-trained comparison models eliminates limited auxiliary training-data coverage; no new evaluation task or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes SFT, SFT + diffu-GRPO, and SFT + TSE-Reward, and adds diffu-GRPO+PRM using a pretrained Mistral-7B reward model on GSM8K and MATH. This substantially changes the comparison scope. TSE-Vote becomes TSE with identical scores, so that is a renamed comparator.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce PRM scoring with reasoning-step tags every 16 timesteps, averaged scores, replacement of NaNs with zeros, and training-speed measurement in seconds per iteration. Retained experiments use the same stated splits, sequence lengths, and training settings. Checkpoint-selection information is newly disclosed rather than established as a changed protocol.

E4.justification: v2 Table 2 adds tests of advantage up-weighting, full versus sampled reward aggregation, and random versus fixed interval endpoints. Figure 4 adds PRM instability and reward-hacking analyses, and Appendix B replaces two COUNTDOWN examples with broader qualitative comparisons. Conversely, GSM8K and MATH training-curve panels are removed; the sample-count ablation remains.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-training-run counts or seeds, or introduces confidence intervals or significance tests. The reward-estimation sample-count ablation and the reporting practices for retained results are unchanged.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores, generalization results, intermediate accuracies, and alignment ratios are unchanged. v2 adds PRM scores, component-ablation results, timings, and qualitative findings; for example, Table 2 reports COUNTDOWN accuracy of 59.4 for Ours-Cover versus 52.0 for Ours at 256 tokens. SFT-related result rows and GSM8K/MATH training diagnostics disappear.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 3's hierarchical selection formulation and Theorem 3.1, together with Appendix B's assumptions, identifiability lemmas, Theorem B.6, and proofs. Separately, v2 Eq. 3 introduces an explicit reward sum over all denoising subintervals, extending v1's interval-reward definition and informal discussion of full-trajectory evaluation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion withdraw the central contribution of identifying a latent reasoning hierarchy and designing SAPO around it. v2 instead centers reward-model-free process supervision, efficient rollout reuse, and reasoning stability. Performance and reasoning-alignment claims remain, while claims concerning additional s1K-trained competitors disappear.

C2.justification: v2 removes the detailed hierarchical mechanism interpretation and the hypothesis that limited model capacity explains weak MATH training gains. It adds interpretations of PRM failures as format/distribution mismatch and reward hacking, explains accuracy-runtime tradeoffs in the new ablations, and expands the discussion of token-dependency and computational limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly reports evaluation every 100 training steps, selection of the best-performing checkpoint, and approximately 72 hours on eight GPUs per dataset. v2 also adds PRM implementation details and dataset provenance/licenses. Access information changes from v1's public code-and-checkpoint link to a statement that training code accompanies supplementary material; actual availability is not verified.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from hierarchical identifiability to process supervision without external reward or value models. v2 adds discussion of MDPO, IGPO, and TraceRL, and cites the PRM used experimentally. The nonlinear-ICA/identifiability references and s1 citation associated with the removed theory and comparisons disappear.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method explanation, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around DPR. The theoretical section disappears, implementation and examples are reorganized across appendices, and limitations, ethical considerations, and LLM-use disclosure receive separate sections. This exceeds simple renaming or renumbering.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. The hierarchy diagram and two appendix example figures disappear; new PRM plots, an ablation/timing table, and three appendix example tables are added. Existing illustrations are relabeled or renumbered, and four-panel training-curve displays are reduced to two panels.

improvement.justification: v2 directly tests reward-design choices that v1 largely motivated without component-level evidence: Table 2 evaluates up-weighting and rollout reuse while quantifying their accuracy-runtime tradeoffs. The PRM comparison and checkpoint-selection disclosure also improve empirical assessment. These gains are limited by removal of s1K-based comparisons and GSM8K/MATH training diagnostics, alongside withdrawal of the theoretical contribution. With the default method and retained benchmark scores unchanged, the net gain is a focused improvement in empirical support and reporting.
